opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the original time horizon work was mostly built on one particular suite of tasks: software engineering and research-flavored tasks that we'd collected and timed with human baselines. And the headline result, that the length of tasks AI agents can complete with 50% reliability has been doubling roughly every seven months, is a really striking trend. But a natural and totally fair objection is: is this just a fact about that specific distribution of tasks? Maybe software is unusually well suited to current models, or maybe our tasks have some quirk that makes the trend look cleaner than it really is.

So extending the methodology to other benchmarks is partly a robustness check. If you take very different domains, like math competition problems, web browsing and computer use, scientific question answering, or self-driving-adjacent things, and you convert performance into this common currency of "how long would this take a skilled human," you can ask whether you see similar exponential trends and similar doubling times. To the extent you do, that's much stronger evidence that something general is going on with AI capabilities, and not just a narrow artifact.

The other thing I find exciting is that time horizon gives you a unit that's actually interpretable and comparable across domains. Benchmark scores like "73% on X" don't mean much on their own, and they saturate: a benchmark goes from 10% to 90% and then it's useless. Translating into human time lets you line up very different benchmarks on the same axis and see where models are relatively stronger or weaker. For example, you might find horizons in some domains are much longer than in others, which tells you something about where capabilities are lopsided, and that's really useful for forecasting when particular kinds of work might become automatable.

There are real caveats, of course. You need decent estimates of human completion time, which many benchmarks don't come with, so you have to approximate. And tasks in benchmarks tend to be cleaner and more self-contained than messy real-world work. But even with those limitations, getting a broader picture of whether this trend generalizes seems like one of the more important empirical questions for understanding how fast things are moving.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that got me excited about the time horizon work in the first place is that it gives you a single axis that's actually interpretable. Most benchmarks, you get a number from zero to one hundred and it's kind of hard to know what that means. Does seventy percent on this thing mean the model is useful? Is eighty percent meaningfully different? Whereas when you say "the model can do tasks that take a human expert about an hour, with fifty percent reliability," that's something you can reason about. You can compare it to what a person does in a day, you can think about what it would mean for a workflow.

The catch is that the original work was pretty heavily weighted toward software engineering and related tasks, because that's where we had good human baselines and tasks that were cleanly specifiable. And I think a lot of people, reasonably, looked at that and said, okay, but is this a fact about AI, or is it a fact about coding? Software is kind of a weird domain. There's a huge amount of training data, there's a tight feedback loop where you can run the tests, and a lot of the tasks decompose really nicely.

So extending it is partly about checking whether the trend is robust. If you measure time horizon in, say, biology research tasks, or math, or something messier like doing a literature review or putting together an analysis from scratch, do you see the same doubling time? Or does it look totally different? Either answer would be interesting. If it generalizes, that's pretty strong evidence that we're measuring something fundamental about agentic capability rather than an artifact of one domain. And if it doesn't generalize, then that tells you something important too, like maybe the thing that's actually driving progress in software is specific to that feedback structure.

And then the other piece, which I think is underrated, is that it forces you to be honest about what the human baselines actually are. A lot of benchmarks don't have serious human baselines at all, or they have one grad student who tried it for an afternoon. To do time horizon properly, you have to go get real experts, time them, and deal with the fact that experts also fail sometimes. That process is annoying, but it's really clarifying, because you end up with a much more grounded sense of what "hard" even means for a given task.

So, yeah. Partly it's about forecasting, partly it's about robustness, and partly it's that I think the methodology itself is just a healthier way to build evaluations.

r001.rationale: The response says extending the methodology to other domains can test whether findings generalize, but it does not identify cybersecurity benchmarks as a domain.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing is that it gives us a more interpretable way to talk about progress. A score going from 40% to 60% on a benchmark can be hard to make sense of. If we can instead say that models are succeeding at tasks that take humans longer and longer, that gives us a better sense of what those improvements mean.

And extending that to more benchmarks would help us understand how general the trend is. Are models handling longer tasks across a broad range of domains, or is that mostly happening in a particular kind of work? I’d be interested in both outcomes. If the trends are similar, that gives us more confidence in the methodology. If they differ, that could tell us something useful about where models still struggle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing is that it gives us a way to translate benchmark performance into something more interpretable. If you tell me a model gets 60 percent on a benchmark, it’s hard to know what that means in practice. If you tell me it can reliably complete tasks that take a human an hour, that gives me a much clearer picture of what it can do.

But we’d like to know how well that picture generalizes. Models might have quite different time horizons for software engineering, scientific research, or other kinds of work. Extending the methodology to more benchmarks would let us test whether we’re seeing a broad increase in the ability to carry out longer tasks, or something more specific to the tasks we’ve measured so far. And that seems useful both for understanding current capabilities and for making better forecasts.

r001.rationale: The response says broader benchmarks would test how well findings generalize, but it does not identify cybersecurity benchmarks as the way to validate them.
